 Judge Delays Decision On Healthcare.Gov Agent Freeze
 October 27, 2026 
 | 
 Source: BenefitsPRO , by Allison Bell 
 A federal judge decided Wednesday to put off making a decision about whether to require HealthCare.gov managers to resume registering new agents and brokers for the open enrollment period for 2027 coverage.
 U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher issued an order giving U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, more time to respond to a request by the National Association of Insurance and Benefits Professionals for a temporary restraining order.
 NABIP asked for the temporary restraining order Oct. 15, when it sued Kennedy and Oz over the HealthCare.gov producer registration moratorium in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland.
 The judge has scheduled a Nov. 5 hearing on the producer registration moratorium, NABIP said.
 “The association will seek to demonstrate why CMS should be required to allow affected agents and brokers to complete the necessary training and registration as soon as possible during open enrollment,” NABIP said.
 Letting HealthCare.gov block or delay the registrations of thousands of agents and brokers will cause irreparable harm to the producers and the producers’ ability to help consumers get covered, NABIP said.
 HHS and CMS said in a response to NABIP’s request for the restraining order that the registration moratorium was announced Sept. 22 and that NABIP did not file its request for a temporary restraining order until three weeks later.
 “NABIP’s asserted injuries are principally financial ones, and their submission fails to demonstrate that these financial injuries constitute irreparable harm requiring issuance of a temporary restraining order,” HHS and CMS said in the response. “These assertions of harm are further belied by NABIP’s delay in seeking emergency relief.”
 HealthCare.gov: HealthCare.gov is part of the family of health insurance exchange programs, or web-based supermarkets for health insurance, created by the Affordable Care Act of 2010.
 HealthCare.gov, which is also called the Marketplace, will help residents of 29 states shop for individual and family health coverage from commercial insurers for 2027 and use federal ACA premium tax credit subsidies to pay for the coverage.
 The HealthCare.gov open enrollment period for 2027 coverage is set to start Nov. 15 and end Jan. 15, 2027.
 HealthCare.gov managers reported in a footnote in an interim final rule published in the Federal Register that HealthCare.gov had 84,012 registered producers in 2026. Officials predicted that the moratorium could affect as many as 19,000 producers who want to start selling the plans distributed by HealthCare.gov in 2027.
 NABIP said in its complaint that it believes producers handled more than 75% of coverage purchases made through HealthCare.gov in 2026.
 HealthCare.gov managers argued that they needed to suspend registrations of new producers because newly registered producers are about three times more likely than returning producers to submit fraudulent coverage applications, and HealthCare.gov needs more time to come up with strategies to address that concern, officials said.
 State regulators’ perspective: The four officers who run the National Association of Insurance Commissioners have written to the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight, the CMS office in charge of HealthCare.gov, to express concerns about the moratorium.
 “Given that open enrollment begins in just a few weeks, we ask that these concerns be considered and resolved in a timely manner,” the NAIC officer said in a public letter about the moratorium. “As your state partners in the enforcement of the Affordable Care Act, and as state officials with responsibility to protect consumers and our markets, we fully support CMS’s goal of eliminating fraud. We have long partnered with CMS to shut down unauthorized sales and plan switching schemes, identify the entities responsible, and take appropriate administrative actions. However, we are concerned about the impact the recently announced moratorium could have on our markets.”
 What it means: The HealthCare.gov producer registration moratorium may hurt companies that offer or administer employer-sponsored Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense arrangement plans, or CHOICE plans, and help at least some plan participants buy coverage through the ACA public exchange system.
 The moratorium could also affect small employers that count on the ACA exchange system to provide coverage for their employees, and, if it hurts 2027 coverage sales, it could affect the viability of the market for commercial health insurance.
 About 186 million U.S. residents now have “private health insurance,” but 110 million are in self-insured employer health plans.
 Only 50 million are in fully insured group health plans, and 20 million have private individual or family health insurance.
 Many of the big, publicly traded health insurers have emphasized their roles as providers of health care services and as administrators of health benefits for government health programs and self-insured employers. New turmoil in the individual health market could further reduce insurers’ interest in the commercial health insurance market and create new opportunities for advocates of single-payer, government-run health finance programs to promote their proposals.
